# How Database Transactions Recover After a Power Failure

When a database server loses power, the situation is fundamentally different from a clean shutdown. The database cannot rely on in-memory state being flushed to disk, because the operating system's page cache and the database's own buffers are lost. What survives is whatever was already written to disk — specifically the write-ahead log (WAL, or redo log) and the on-disk data files. Recovery after a power failure is therefore a log-driven process: the database reconstructs the correct state from the log, not from memory. # How a Compiler Detects and Optimizes Repeated Expressions

Repeated expressions are one of the most common sources of wasted computation in programs. A compiler that can recognize that two computations are equivalent can eliminate redundant work, sometimes turning an O(n²) loop into an O(n) one. # How TCP Congestion Control Adapts to Changing Bandwidth

TCP congestion control is the set of algorithms a TCP sender uses to infer the available capacity of the network path and to adjust its sending rate accordingly. Because the network is a black box—the sender cannot directly measure link bandwidth or queue occupancy—TCP relies on feedback signals: acknowledgments (ACKs) and, in modern stacks, selective ACK (SACK) information, RTT measurements, and ECN/CE marks.
